children.text: A curving white sand beach about
1 km

long in front of San Isidro village, west of Puerto Galera town. Days are for swimming, banana boats and island hopping; at sunset come seafood dinners on the sand, then Mindoro Sling and live music — this is the weekend beach Manila residents head to most.
White Beach is a bow-shaped stretch of white sand in front of San Isidro village, on the western side of Puerto Galera at the northern tip of Mindoro. It runs about
1 km

from its southwestern to its northeastern end, closed off at both ends by wooded rocky headlands, with green mountains rising right behind it. The water in front is the Verde Island Passage between Luzon and Mindoro, and on clear days you can see the mountains of Batangas across the strait. It is just
10–20 minutes
by tricycle from Balatero Port, where the ferries arrive, so many visitors to Puerto Galera base themselves here.

Puerto Galera has several beaches, each with its own character. If Sabang to the east, packed with dive centers, is the divers' base, White Beach is the swimming and party beach where Filipino college students and families flock. Along the beach, a single row of resorts, restaurants, bars, souvenir stalls and tattoo shops sits on a concrete embankment a few steps back from the water, and after sunset tables and music spill out onto the sand in front. Dive sites and the town as a whole are covered separately under
Puerto Galera

The crowds brought environmental problems too. After high coliform contamination was found in the coastal waters, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) inspected 559 establishments in
April 2018
and ordered 10 in Sabang and 3 around White Beach that encroached on the coastal easement to demolish their structures themselves within
30 days
. With so many people coming, the coastal easement and sewage treatment remain issues the town and environmental authorities keep watching.
On
February 28, 2023
, the tanker Princess Empress, carrying about 800,000 liters of industrial oil, sank off Naujan in Oriental Mindoro, and Puerto Galera was hit hard as well. In
April 2023

, DENR and Department of Health tests found that only 9 of 35 shoreline sites in Puerto Galera met the oil and grease standard, and West San Isidro Bay was among those that passed. The Department of Tourism said there was no swimming ban; the fishing ban in Puerto Galera was lifted on
, and in
June 2023
the Coast Guard finished recovering oil from the sunken tanker. Visitors have since returned, and the provincial government reported that about 250,000 people visited Puerto Galera in
January–April 2026
alone, surpassing pre-pandemic levels.

It suits Manila workers looking for the sea on weekends, groups of friends who want a lively time, and families who want to swim in shallow water and try water sports. If you prefer a quiet beach, you can stay at Aninuan or Talipanan Beach farther west and come to White Beach only in the evening. In
March–May
, when Holy Week and the summer school break overlap, the beach is packed, so go on a weekday if you want some space.
Around
6–7 AM

, before the beach wakes up, White Beach is a completely different place from daytime. There are few people on the sand and only a few fishing boats on the water, so you can take in the whole beach out to the rocky headlands at both ends, and the clouds hanging on the mountains behind it are at their clearest. It is also the best time for photos.

The shore generally slopes gently, making it a good place to swim with children. There is little coral worth seeing right off the beach, though, so for real snorkeling you need to go out by boat, and keep away from the areas where banana boats and jet skis run.
You can sign up for water sports right at the beach booths. A short banana boat ride costs about
per boat (1–10 people), parasailing about
for one person or about
for two (about
15 minutes
), and a jet ski about
for
30 minutes
. Prices and times vary a little from booth to booth, so check the ride time and life jackets first.
At the beach tour booths you can hire a bangka for an island-hopping trip around the coral garden, the giant clam sanctuary and small beaches. A boat (up to 6 people) costs about
, each extra person adds about
, and transferring to a small boat at the sanctuary costs about
per person on top.

blocks.title: Sunset and seafood dinner on the sand

children.text: As the sun goes down, the sea and sky turn orange, and the restaurants lay out fish, shrimp, squid and crab on ice. Pick what you want and they price it by weight and grill or stir-fry it for you, so ask the price per weight and the cooking charge before ordering. Grab a table by the water about
30 minutes
before the sunset begins.

Mindoro Sling, Puerto Galera's signature cocktail, is a sweet drink of Tanduay rum mixed with mango and orange juice, Sprite and grenadine, with apple and orange slices floating on top. It is usually ordered by the pitcher and shared, but the juice hides the alcohol and it hits you late, so drink slowly.
After dark, acoustic and reggae bands start playing at the bars, and the atmosphere is liveliest between
7 PM and 2 AM
. Fire dancing happens on the sand mostly on Friday and weekend nights with no fixed schedule, and it is customary to give the performers a small tip afterward.

blocks.title: Aninuan and Talipanan beaches and waterfalls

children.text: Aninuan Beach, about
1 km
to the west, and Talipanan Beach, about
2 km
away, are much quieter than White Beach. From near the Aninuan bridge, the forest trail to Aninuan Falls takes about
1 hour
; the trail to Talipanan Falls, through a Mangyan village, is easier, but the falls are small. Go with a local guide when passing through the village, and an entrance fee may be charged.

For a

trip, do the morning island hopping on day 2 and head straight to Balatero Port after lunch. Return boats usually stop around
3–4 PM
, so don't count on the last boat; take one or two departures earlier.
Air-conditioned buses to Batangas Port, including JAM Liner and DLTB, leave frequently from early morning around Cubao and Buendia (Pasay) in Manila. Depending on traffic, the trip takes about
2–3 hours 30 minutes
and costs about

Boats to Puerto Galera leave from Passenger Terminal Building 3 (PTB 3) at Batangas Port. When you get off the bus, go straight to the shipping line counters inside the port, and avoid touts outside the port who offer to buy tickets for you.
Boats run by Island Water, Montenegro Lines, Galerian and others leave several times a day from around
6 AM
to around
. The fast craft takes about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
and costs about
one way; the RoRo ferry takes about
2 hours

environmental user fee at the municipal desk in Balatero Port. Students, seniors, people with disabilities and some others get a 20% discount with valid ID. Register on the municipal tourism office's PG-Pass site before you leave to get a QR code and skip the queue. Fees and procedures change often, so check the latest notices.
There is currently no boat straight to White Beach. Large bangkas once ran from Batangas Port, stopping at Sabang before dropping passengers right onto the sand at White Beach, and a
PhilGo travelogue records this, but by around
they had already disappeared. All public passenger vessels now dock at Balatero Port, so do not take private boats advertising "direct to White Beach."
Tricycles and electric tuk-tuks wait outside Balatero Port. The ride to White Beach takes about
10–20 minutes
, and the charter fare quoted by the municipal tourism office is about
per vehicle. With around three passengers you can sometimes bargain it down to about
, so agree on the price before getting in.
If you miss the boat to Balatero, take the Batangas–Calapan RoRo ferry, which runs all day (about
2 hours
, about

1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
From town to White Beach, a tricycle takes about
15 minutes
and costs about
. Even overland arrivals pay the environmental user fee at the Villaflor boundary, so register on PG-Pass the same way.
You can walk everywhere along the beach. Tricycles always wait on the village road behind the beach, so hail one to go to Aninuan or Talipanan Beach or into town.
Sabang, the diving hub, is about
30 minutes
away by jeepney or tricycle. Motorbikes can be rented for about
a day, but the hill roads are steep, so ride only if you are a confident driver.
The best time for White Beach is the dry season,
November–May
December–January

April–May
daytime temperatures climb to about
. The sea is coolest in
January–March
at about
, and from
April
it warms to about
, ideal for swimming.
June–October
is the rainy season, and in
July–October
the southwest monsoon (habagat) and typhoons combine to bring high waves. In
August
in particular, big swells can make swimming dangerous on some days, and the Batangas route sometimes stops altogether. During Typhoon Inday in
July 2026
, all Batangas–Puerto Galera trips were canceled. In this season, check the weather forecast and Coast Guard and shipping line notices, and leave slack around your return date.

The busiest times are the Holy Week holidays, the summer school break, and the Christmas and New Year holidays. Passengers then crowd Batangas Port, tickets sell out early and beach lodging prices rise sharply, so book your room first and set off early on a dawn bus. By contrast,
November
and weekdays outside Holy Week bring good weather and a quiet beach.

Lodging falls into three bands: the row right on the beach, the alleys behind it, and the hillside. Beachfront rooms open straight onto the sand but hear music late into the night, while rooms down the alleys or at either end of the beach are much quieter. As of
, simple rooms cost about
a night, mid-range hotels with air conditioning and a pool about
, and boutique resorts about
; prices go up and rooms fill early on Holy Week, year-end and summer-break weekends.

If you follow touts handing out flyers at the port, you are likely to end up in a run-down room with a commission added. Book ahead and save your confirmation on your phone. For a short rest on a day trip, ask around: some resorts rent rooms by the hour or let you use just the showers.

Seafood barbecue is the heart of the food scene. Pick fish, shrimp and squid off the ice to be grilled, and add charcoal-grilled pork skewers, sizzling sisig or kinilaw, fish cured in vinegar. Restaurants facing the sea also serve pizza, pasta and steak, but at prices well above the city. Mindoro Sling is the signature drink, and mango shakes are popular during the day. At the small local eateries (carinderias) on the village road behind the beach, a meal of rice and side dishes costs much less.
Register on PG-Pass before you leave to get your QR code, and carry your ID and hotel booking confirmation. Online registration takes
2–5 minutes
; manual registration on site takes longer.
Puerto Galera has few ATMs, and they can run out of cash in peak season. Withdraw plenty of cash in Batangas or Manila and bring small bills.
On your return day, don't aim for the last boat; take a morning or early-afternoon departure. Afternoon boats can be canceled suddenly when the weather turns.
For water sports and island hopping, confirm the price, ride time, number of people and whether sanctuary fees are included, and when you pay, get a receipt or a note with the details.
For a quiet stay, choose lodging at either end of the beach or down the alleys rather than in the middle. Bar music can go on until around
2 AM
Wear water shoes when snorkeling. Sea urchins are common, and stepping on coral hurts both the coral and your feet.
If you worry about seasickness, take motion-sickness medicine
30 minutes
before departure and sit near the middle of the boat, where it rocks least. Keep your phone and wallet in a waterproof pouch so sea spray is no worry.
Photos are best in the early morning, when few people are around, and at sunset. If you fly a drone, avoid flying over crowds.

The Batangas–Puerto Galera route stops without warning when waves are high, and once it stops you can be stuck for a day or two. Check Coast Guard and shipping line notices before you set out and on the morning of your return, and if you have a flight or work the next day, move your schedule a day earlier.
Don't swim where banana boats and jet skis operate; enter the water only within the lifeguard flags and buoys. Never swim at night after drinking.
Around the bars at night, don't leave your phone and wallet on the table, and never take your eyes off your drink. Check the price of drinks and the per-weight price of seafood before ordering.

Buy boat tickets and pay the environmental user fee only at the official port counters, the municipal desk or the PG-Pass site. Tickets sold by touts and private "direct" boats may be overpriced or fall short of safety standards.
Since the

oil spill, water quality testing and swimming advisories can still change by season and location. Check the latest notices from the municipal tourism office and your lodging before going in the water.
Touching or taking coral, giant clams or sea turtles is prohibited. Don't leave trash on the beach; carry plastic back to your lodging to throw away.
